text: Hong Kong does not differentiate by EU status. The categories are 'local' and 'non-local'; a Danish student is non-local.
Danish SU: a full degree outside the EU/EEA follows separate rules. Check su.dk before budgeting.
Given the fee level, a scholarship is not a nice extra in Hong Kong — for most Danish families it is the difference between viable and not. Apply for everything, and apply in the first round.

Non-local students are normally required to hold medical insurance, often arranged through the university as a compulsory charge. Public healthcare in Hong Kong is available to non-residents at a higher non-eligible-persons rate, which is substantial for anything serious. Your Danish EHIC does not apply. Check what the university's scheme covers and top it up.
The route for a Danish IB student is the 'non-JUPAS' or 'international qualifications' route. JUPAS is the domestic system for Hong Kong DSE students and is not relevant to you.
Four years of tuition alone comes to roughly HK$0.9–1.1 million at 2027/28 fees (medicine and dentistry excepted) — about DKK 770,000 to 940,000 at September 2026 exchange rates.
Hong Kong's four-year degree means an extra year compared with a three-year Danish, Dutch or British bachelor's — factor that into the total cost.
Denmark's SU works differently for a full degree outside the EU/EEA. Check su.dk before budgeting.

Hungary does have a central admissions system, and it is not the one an IB student from Denmark normally uses: felvi.hu / E-felvételi handles Hungarian-language and state-funded places, while the English-taught programmes on this page are applied for directly to each university. felvi states the rule in Hungarian rather than publishing a 2027 date: "a szeptemberben induló képzésekre vonatkozó általános felvételi eljárás meghirdetései legkésőbb az előző év december 31-ig jelennek meg honlapunkon, a jelentkezési határidő többnyire a rákövetkező év február 15-én jár le" - the programmes are announced by 31 December of the previous year at the latest and the application deadline usually falls on 15 February, with the point thresholds (ponthatárok) set in July. "Többnyire" is felvi’s own hedge, which is why no date is recorded. Semmelweis puts the division plainly from the other side: "Our English language programs are fundamentally available for applicants having no Hungarian citizenship as the Hungarian citizens are eligible to apply for the Hungarian language programs through FELVI." Read in Hungarian on 23 September 2026.

Published with its year: "Entrance exams are organized each Wednesday between 3rd March and 14th July 2027." The window runs weekly, not continuously - there are twenty Wednesdays in it and you sit one of them. Register two weeks in advance. Exams can be sat in Pécs, in Budapest at McDaniel College, or abroad through representative agencies, and there is a 250 USD entrance exam fee on top of the application fee.
Work out the funding first. There is no Hungarian scholarship open to a Danish citizen, so budget the full tuition plus living costs before you commit to anything.

Danish SU for a full degree abroad, at DKK 7,426 a month before tax for students living away from home in 2026. Hungary is not a Nordic country for SU purposes, so support is capped at four years — which does not cover a six-year medical degree. Plan for that gap.

Stipendium Hungaricum is closed to you. It operates through bilateral sending-partner agreements and requires nomination by your country's designated authority. No EU member state appears on the partner list — the only European entries are non-EU countries in the Western Balkans plus Moldova, Ukraine, Belarus, Russia, Georgia, Armenia and Türkiye.

The Hungarian Diaspora Scholarship is also closed to you. It is open only to members of the Hungarian diaspora residing outside the European Union, so Hungarian ancestry does not help if you live in Denmark.
A realistic conclusion: a Danish IB student in Hungary is self-funded, with Danish SU as the only meaningful support.

Bring your Danish EHIC. As an EU citizen you are covered on the same terms as a Hungarian, with the same rights and obligations. Students on exchange or at a state-run institute get free medical care; students who do not meet those criteria can sign an agreement with the Hungarian Health Insurance Fund at a cost of 30 percent of the local minimum wage. Note that the EHIC covers medically necessary state-provided care, not comprehensive private cover. Whether an EU student needs a Hungarian TAJ social security card alongside the EHIC is not confirmed here — the official healthcare page does not mention it; ask your university.

Hungary's oldest university by founding date and the only medical school with 2027-entry exam dates already published — every Wednesday from 3 March to 14 July 2027. Its fee page is also labelled 2027/28, which makes it the best-dated source in the country. You can sit the exam in Pécs, in Budapest, or abroad through a representative agency. Its 2027 application deadline and its position on the IB were not published.

Hungary is where Scandinavians go to study medicine in English, and its four medical universities - Semmelweis, Debrecen, Pécs and Szeged - are genuinely open to you. What you need to understand before anything else is the money. Hungary's big scholarships — Stipendium Hungaricum and the Diaspora Scholarship — are both closed to EU citizens, and Denmark is not on the list for Hungary's bilateral state scholarships either. As a Danish student you are self-funded, and a medical degree costs roughly 15,000 to 19,000 euros a year for six years. The one piece of good news: Szeged waives its medicine entrance exam entirely if your IB has a 5 in two Higher Level sciences.

Four universities - Semmelweis, Debrecen, Pécs and Szeged - teach medicine fully in English, most also dentistry and pharmacy, and Univet teaches veterinary medicine; many entrance exams can be sat online from Denmark.
As an EU student you have unlimited work rights once you hold a registration card, and your Danish EHIC gives you healthcare on the same terms as a Hungarian.

Free Fees Initiative: the state pays your tuition if you are an EU/EEA/Swiss/UK national who has been ordinarily resident in an EU/EEA/Swiss state or the UK for at least three of the five years before entry, on a first full-time undergraduate course of at least two years. A Danish student who has lived in Denmark qualifies on the residency test.
Danish SU: as a Danish citizen you can normally take SU abroad for a full degree. Apply to Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen in good time.

SUSI grants cover the student contribution for students who meet Irish means and residency tests. Most students moving from Denmark will not meet the residency condition in their first year, so do not plan around it.

Bring your European Health Insurance Card from Denmark; it covers medically necessary public treatment during your stay. EU students are not required to buy private health insurance. Note that Ireland charges for GP visits unless you qualify for a medical card or GP visit card, so budget for that, and most universities run a low-cost student health service on campus. Non-EU students must hold private health insurance as a condition of their immigration permission.
A green campus in Ireland's second city, strong in food, pharma and life sciences with a big multinational employer base nearby.
Primary school teaching requires Irish, which effectively closes that route to an IB student from Denmark.

Nothing to arrange in advance as an EU citizen: you can enter with your Danish passport or national ID card and stay to study with no visa or residence permit. Once you arrive, get a PPS number (Personal Public Service number) from the Department of Social Protection - you need it for a job, a bank account and most public services - and open an Irish bank account. Non-EU students need a visa or preclearance before travelling and must register with immigration and pay the residence permit fee.

Published as "1 February" with no year; the year here is inferred from the intake this profile covers. Certified academic transcripts and previous degree diplomas must reach the university by the same day. The application period opens "around mid December", published without a precise day, so there is no opening date here to count down to. Both the deadline page and the FAQ agree that 1 February is the date for an international applicant — and those are the same two pages that contradict each other about 5 June, which is why this is the safe deadline for a Danish applicant.

Published as "April 30th" with no year; the year here is inferred from the intake this profile covers. The window opens on 5 February, which is its own entry. Non-EU/EEA residents run a separate and much earlier cycle — open 5 October, close 31 January, autumn semester only — which does not apply to a Danish citizen.

The University of Iceland's own two pages disagree about who can use 5 June. The deadline page (https://english.hi.is/study/apply/application-deadline) lists the autumn undergraduate deadline of 5 June under "Icelandic and Nordic citizens", which would include a Dane applying from Denmark. The FAQ (https://english.hi.is/faq/when-application-deadline) gives the same 5 June only to "International students who have lived in Iceland og are living in Iceland" and does not mention Nordic citizens; the untranslated Icelandic "og" suggests it is a partial translation that has fallen out of step with the deadline page. Both pages were live on 23 September 2026. If you rely on 5 June and the stricter reading is the right one, you lose a year, so no date is counted down here. Apply by 1 February 2027, which both pages agree is open to you, and if you want to use 5 June, get it confirmed in writing by admission@hi.is before you rely on it.

Published as "open at the beginning of March until June 5th" with no year; the year here is inferred from the intake this profile covers. The March opening is published without a day, so there is no opening date to record. Akureyri says "EU/EEA residents" where the University of Iceland says "Nordic citizens", and unlike Iceland it says the same thing in one place only — there is no second Akureyri page to contradict it. Non-EEA applicants have earlier deadlines, 1 March for Polar Law and 1 April for everything else, and pay a 50-euro application fee; neither applies to a Danish citizen.

Danish SU for a full degree abroad, at DKK 7,426 a month before tax for students living away from home in 2026. Because Iceland is a Nordic country, SU is paid as if you studied in Denmark, not capped at four years. Under the SU reform that takes effect on 1 January 2027, anyone starting after 1 July 2025 gets SU for the programme's prescribed length only. Apply through minSU Fast Track no later than the first month you want support for, and document your progress twice a year.

Menntasjóður námsmanna, the Icelandic student loan fund, appears to be directly open to you. Its rules list being a citizen of Denmark, Finland, Norway or Sweden as a standalone qualifying condition, with no work or residency requirement attached — unlike other EEA citizens, who must work at least 40 hours a month in Iceland. This is more generous than most Nordic funds, so confirm it with the fund before relying on it.
You cannot take both. Menntasjóður states that students cannot receive an Icelandic student loan while receiving study assistance from another state, which includes Danish SU. It is one or the other.

As a Nordic student you have the easiest position of anyone: Study in Iceland says Nordic students need only confirmation of insurance in their home country, such as a health insurance card. Bring your Danish EHIC and present it with your passport at medical visits. There is a widely repeated claim that Icelandic Health Insurance only begins after six months of legal domicile. That could not be confirmed on any official page, though the fact that Menntasjóður lends up to ISK 550,000 a year for health insurance costs suggests a real gap exists. Non-EU students must have insurance in place before arrival.

Not required at all if you hold an IB Diploma — the University of Iceland's IB page says so directly. Its Denmark page also accepts a Danish studentereksamen, HHX or HTX with English. Reykjavik University, for its English-taught graduate provision, asks for TOEFL iBT 91, IELTS Academic 6.5, DAAD B2 or Cambridge B2.

Reykjavik University's Computer Science BSc page says: taught in Icelandic, proficiency in Icelandic is a requirement, and applications from abroad are not accepted. Its Business Administration BSc requires Icelandic even though all third-year teaching is in English.
SU — studies abroad
SU — hvad kan du få (SU til en hel uddannelse i udlandet)
SU — the SU reform in English

Across Iceland's six universities only three bachelor's degrees are described as taught in English: International Studies in Education and English Studies, both BAs at the University of Iceland, and Contemporary Dance Practices, BA at the Iceland University of the Arts. Every other bachelor's programme in Iceland is taught in Icelandic, and several explicitly demand Icelandic proficiency or refuse applications from abroad altogether. Iceland is a realistic destination for an exchange semester or a master's degree, and only a very narrow one for an undergraduate degree in English.

For international applicants the University of Iceland deadline is 1 February, a full six months before you start. Two of its own pages disagree about whether Danish citizens can instead use the 5 June Nordic deadline, so apply by 1 February and email admission@hi.is to check.

Reykjavik University publishes undergraduate tuition of ISK 1,794,000 a year for non-EEA students while its bachelor teaching is in Icelandic and one department says it does not accept applications from abroad. Email admissions@ru.is before assuming any English route exists.
Danish SU travels here on Nordic terms: paid as if you studied in Denmark, rather than capped at the four years that apply outside the Nordics.
Danish students face no English test at all. The University of Iceland's IB page says English proficiency is 'Not required' for IB Diploma holders.
EEA citizens, including Danes, need no work permit in Iceland. Non-EEA students need a work permit, and the weekly hour limit is not confirmed here.

Set in the MUR/MAECI circular "Procedure per l'ingresso, il soggiorno, l'immatricolazione degli studenti internazionali", which is explicitly valid for two years: "VALIDE PER GLI ANNI ACCADEMICI 2026-2027 e 2027-2028". Its wording is "Per l'anno accademico 2027/2028 [...] il termine ultimo per la presentazione delle domande di visto è fissato al 31 ottobre 2027"; the 2026/27 equivalent in the same paragraph is "entro e non oltre il 30 novembre 2026". Note what the date actually is: it is the last day to lodge the visa application at the consulate, and the Universitaly pre-enrolment has to be submitted and validated by the university before that — the circular adds that institutions may set their own earlier dates, "Tali date potranno essere anche antecedenti a quella del 30 novembre 2026 e del 31 ottobre 2027". None of it applies to a Danish citizen: the circular lists among those the visa procedures do not apply to "i cittadini appartenenti ai Paesi dell'Unione Europea, nonché a quelli provenienti da Norvegia, Islanda, Lichtenstein e alla Confederazione Elvetica, alla Repubblica di San Marino e alla Santa Sede". Listed for completeness only.
If you want the income-based fee, apply for an ISEE parificato through an affiliated Italian CAF office, with your family's Danish income and property documents legalised and translated into Italian.

How ISEE works for a foreign family: ISEE is an Italian means-test combining household income (from two years before), savings and property, divided by a scale based on household size. Because your family's income and property are in Denmark, you cannot get an ordinary ISEE. Instead you request an ISEE parificato (also written ISEEU parificato) from an affiliated Italian tax-assistance centre, a CAF. You supply household composition, each member's income for the second preceding year, certificates for any property owned on 31 December, and any securities or shareholdings. Foreign documents must be legalised by an Italian diplomatic or consular representation and accompanied by a certified Italian translation. The CAF sends the result straight to the university. If you skip this step, the university assumes you are wealthy and bills the top bracket.
Danish SU can be taken abroad for a full degree if the programme is approved by Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen — check su.dk before you commit.

As a Danish citizen you enter on your passport or national ID card. If you stay longer than three months you register as an EU resident (iscrizione anagrafica) at the comune where you live, showing enrolment, health cover and evidence of sufficient means. You will also want a codice fiscale (tax code) almost immediately — banks, phone contracts, rental agreements and the university all ask for it.
Politecnico di Milano — students with income and property abroad (ISEEU parificato)

Italy has no single national application system for EU students. You apply to each university on its own portal, and for many degrees you also sit an online entrance test called a TOLC. The big surprise is money: public universities charge you according to your family's income, not a flat fee, so a Danish family on a normal income often pays a few hundred to a couple of thousand euros a year. English-taught bachelor's degrees exist but are a minority, concentrated in economics, engineering, design and international relations.
Getting the income-based fee as a foreign family means obtaining an ISEE parificato through an Italian CAF office, with legalised and translated Danish income documents — start this months early
Living costs outside Milan (Bologna, Padova, Torino, Trento) are low by Danish standards

No undergraduate MEXT call appears on the Embassy of Japan in Denmark’s site: its news list for the whole of 2026 carries exactly one MEXT call, for Research Students, with an application deadline of 15 June 2026. MEXT’s national rule — recruitment in April and May of the year before arrival — therefore describes a window a Danish IB candidate cannot use through this embassy. Because this rests on what the embassy's site does not list, write to the embassy at info@ch.mofa.go.jp before relying on it either way. The route that plausibly remains open to a school-leaver is university-recommendation MEXT, after admission.
The Embassy of Japan in Denmark offers Danish nationals only the Japanese Studies and Research Student scholarships, and both are for students already at university.

Do not build a MEXT application into the plan without checking first. The Embassy of Japan in Copenhagen offers Danish nationals only the Japanese Studies and Research Student types, both of which require you to be at university already, and ran no undergraduate call in 2026. Ask info@ch.mofa.go.jp directly. The route that is open to a school-leaver is university-recommendation MEXT, which the university nominates you for after admitting you — so ask each admissions office whether it holds quota places.

MEXT (Monbukagakusho) Undergraduate Scholarship — nationally this is five years from April, one of them a preparatory year in Japanese, 117,000 yen a month, entrance examination, matriculation and tuition fees waived, and an economy air ticket each way, with all classes in Japanese except where a grantee is directly placed at a university requiring none, and with MEXT rather than the student choosing the university. It is listed because people ask about it, not because it is available: the Embassy of Japan in Copenhagen lists only two MEXT types for Danish nationals, Japanese Studies and Research Student, and neither is this one. On a Danish passport, from a Danish gymnasium, treat the embassy track as closed until the embassy tells you otherwise in writing.

University-recommendation MEXT places — some universities nominate their own admitted students, and for a Danish school-leaver this is the only MEXT route that plausibly remains open, since it runs through the university rather than the embassy. Ask each admissions office whether it holds MEXT quota places and how a new international entrant is considered for one.
Danish SU: studying for a full degree outside the EU/EEA follows different rules from studying inside it. Check su.dk before assuming SU will travel with you.

Enrolment in Japan's National Health Insurance is compulsory for anyone staying more than three months and is arranged at the municipal office when you register. It covers roughly 70% of medical costs; students typically add the university's own supplementary cover. Your Danish EHIC does not apply in Japan.

Most English-taught programmes guarantee or strongly prioritise first-year places in a university dormitory or international house, which is by far the easiest route and usually cheaper than the private market. APU houses all first-year international students in AP House. Private renting in Japan involves key money, guarantor requirements and agency fees that are difficult to navigate from abroad — take the dormitory.

MEXT's scholarship route applies its own academic condition — twelve years of schooling completed by March of the arrival year, or by August where the applicant enters in the autumn term through direct placement. A Danish gymnasium finishing in June sits between the two. This is now a secondary question, because the Embassy of Japan in Copenhagen does not appear to run the undergraduate embassy track for Danish nationals at all; see the deadline entry for what it publishes.

All teaching is in English. One undergraduate degree programme with three courses: Global Business, Global Studies and Global Connectivity. April and September intakes. A year abroad is compulsory for every student.

A small public university in northern Japan where every class is in English. Every student spends a year at a partner university abroad, and it is known for its 24-hour library and strong graduate employment.
Embassy of Japan in Denmark — Study in Japan (lists only Japanese Studies and Research Student MEXT types for Danish nationals)
Embassy of Japan in Denmark — Invitation for Application: Japanese Government Scholarship for Research Students 2027 (the embassy's only MEXT call of 2026)

The MEXT undergraduate scholarship is not open to you from Denmark. The Embassy of Japan in Copenhagen states on its Study in Japan page that there are two types of MEXT programme for Danish nationals — Japanese Studies, for students already majoring in Japanese studies at a university, and Research Student, for graduate study — and the Undergraduate scholarship is not one of them. Its entire 2026 news list carries a single MEXT call, for Research Students 2027, with a deadline of 15 June 2026. Plan Japan's finances around institutional awards and JASSO, not around MEXT, and if MEXT matters to you, write to info@ch.mofa.go.jp and get the position in writing before you build a year around it.
Denmark's SU does not follow you to Japan on the same terms as an EU/EEA country. Check with su.dk early; a full degree outside the EU/EEA has separate rules.

Keio's PEARL runs three application periods for September 2027, the last closing on 7 April 2027, and accepts predicted IB grades in as many words. It is the latest Japanese deadline on this page and the one that fits a Danish school year.

Money at the point of admission rather than by separate application: Waseda states that its scholarship recipients are determined by the admission result with no separate form, and Kyoto's iUP attaches fee waivers and monthly scholarships to eligible students. This matters more here than MEXT does, because the MEXT undergraduate scholarship is not offered to Danish nationals — see the watch-outs.

If you want the Global Korea Scholarship, read the invited-country list first. On a Danish passport only the University Track's UIC Program is open, and it is science and engineering at thirteen named universities. Applying on more than one track voids the application.

Dormitory places are cheap and usually available to first-year international students. Off-campus renting in Korea involves a large jeonse or wolse key deposit that is difficult to raise from abroad — take the dormitory.

Global Korea Scholarship (GKS), run by NIIED — the Korean government's scholarship for undergraduate degrees, and smaller than it looks from Denmark. The 2027 round covers tuition of up to 5m KRW a semester, a Korean language year costing 5.2m KRW, airfare, and an allowance of 13.56m KRW in the language year and 14.4m KRW a year during the degree, over five to seven years. The Embassy Track invites 74 countries and Denmark is not among them; only the University Track's UIC Program, science and engineering at thirteen named universities, is open to a Danish citizen. A May 2027 IB graduate is in any case ineligible for the 2027 round, which requires a graduation certificate by 31 December 2026 — the round to plan for is 2028.
Danish SU: a full degree outside the EU/EEA follows separate rules. Check su.dk before assuming SU travels with you.

International students staying more than six months are enrolled in Korea's National Health Insurance Service, with a monthly premium deducted or billed. It is compulsory and it is good — Korean healthcare is fast and inexpensive at the point of use. Your Danish EHIC does not apply.

University dormitories are the standard and by far the easiest route for a first-year international student: cheap, on campus, and allocated with the admission. The private market in Seoul requires a large up-front deposit (jeonse or wolse) that is impractical to arrange from Denmark. Apply for the dormitory the moment your offer arrives — places at Yonsei and Korea University are oversubscribed.

The relevant Korean category is the '12-year education completed entirely outside Korea' route, which an IB Diploma from a Danish gymnasium satisfies. This is the track that removes the Suneung from the equation.

The Global Korea Scholarship's Embassy Track is closed to Danish citizens. The 2027 guidelines invite 74 countries and Denmark is not one of them, and no Korean embassy in Denmark appears in the guidelines' own contact list. Only the University Track's UIC Program is open — science and engineering at thirteen named universities, none of them Yonsei, KAIST, Seoul National or Korea University.
Denmark's SU works differently for a full degree outside the EU/EEA. Confirm with su.dk before budgeting.

Vilnius University is the university this profile sends you to first. It has one intake a year and splits the deadline by citizenship. For autumn 2026 the page read: "1 May for applicants from non-EU/EFTA countries" and "1 July for applicants who are citizens of EU/EFTA countries and for non-EU/EFTA applicants with a 90-day visa-free period that has not yet been exceeded". A Danish citizen is in the July group. The 2027 dates were not published on 23 September 2026 - admissions.vu.lt offered only a "Get 2027 Admissions Updates" sign-up - so no date is recorded here. Two things that are not dates but behave like them: the application fee is 100 EUR, non-refundable, and "An online application will be processed only after the application fee is collected and the application is submitted with all the required documents", so an unpaid invoice on the closing day is a missed deadline; and admission can close early, because the published deadline runs only until the limit of study places is reached. EU and EFTA citizens may apply for state-funded as well as fee-paying places.

This is the ISM deadline that actually applies to a Danish applicant. ISM runs main admission twice, on different dates for different passports: "Main admission. For candidates from visa regime countries (May 1 - May 31)", closing 31 May with the contract signed by 12 June, and "Main admission. For candidates from visa - free regime and CIS countries (May 1 - July 24)", closing 24 July with the contract signed by 31 July. An EU citizen is in the second group and has nearly two more months than the first. Rolled forward from the 2026 calendar, which was still the one published on 23 September 2026.

Check which deadline is yours. ISM and Vilnius both publish different closing dates for visa-free and visa-required applicants, and as a Danish citizen you get the later one, but only if you read the right line. In 2026 that was 24 July at ISM and 1 July at Vilnius; neither has confirmed its 2027 dates yet.
Danish SU for a full degree abroad requires approval of the programme by Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen - confirm with your studievejleder.

Study in Lithuania states applicants need 'a diploma of secondary education (school leaving certificate or corresponding document from your country certified by the Centre for Quality Assessment in Higher Education)'.

As a Danish or other EU citizen you have the right to live and study in Lithuania and complete a residence registration for stays over three months. Non-EU students need a national visa and a temporary residence permit arranged before travelling; Vilnius University keeps a dedicated page on visas and residence permits. The precise EU registration procedure is not confirmed here; ask your university's international office.
EU citizens, including Danes
Plan for the compulsory semester abroad, normally taken in the third, fourth or fifth semester.
Danish SU taken abroad is the realistic backbone of your funding - apply to Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen before you leave.

Bring your European Health Insurance Card from Denmark. If you register as a resident and study in Luxembourg for a full degree, you will normally be affiliated to the Luxembourg health insurance system (CNS) - the university's student department explains the process during enrolment. Non-EU students must show proof of health cover to obtain their residence permit.

The hardest practical problem of studying in Luxembourg. The country has one of the most expensive rental markets in the EU and the student population competes with a large professional and cross-border workforce. The University of Luxembourg runs its own student housing service and this should be your first and main approach - apply as soon as you are admitted, not after. If you miss university housing, consider living just across the border in France, Germany or Belgium and commuting: public transport inside Luxembourg is free, and many students in the Greater Region do exactly this. No official rent figures are quoted here.
The country's only public university, built on a redeveloped steelworks site at Belval, with a compulsory semester abroad in every bachelor's degree.

As an EU citizen you enter with your Danish passport or ID card and need no visa. You must make a declaration of arrival at the commune where you live, and after three months register as an EU citizen residing in Luxembourg, showing proof of enrolment, sufficient resources and health cover. Non-EU students need a temporary authorisation to stay before travelling, followed by a residence permit after arrival.
Guichet.lu - Doing a semester abroad from the University of Luxembourg (compulsory mobility semester, waivers and exemptions)

Luxembourg has essentially one public university, founded in 2003, and it is unlike anywhere else on this site. Programmes are multilingual by design - many bachelor's are taught in two languages, typically French and English or French and German - and every bachelor student has to spend a semester abroad, which is written into the rules rather than offered as an option. It is small, well funded, and sits at the centre of EU institutions and international finance. The country is also one of the most expensive in Europe to live in, and there is only one annual intake, in September.
One small multilingual university, and a semester abroad built in
A compulsory semester abroad in every bachelor's degree, so international mobility is guaranteed rather than something you have to organise.

Selection is per programme. Medicine and dentistry at RSU are competitive and close earlier for non-EU applicants. SSE Riga is the most selective route in the country: it requires minimum grades of 6 on a scale of 10 in Mathematics and English, runs its own admissions test covering mathematical reasoning, logical thinking and English, interviews the top performers, and takes 150 students. Latvia does operate state-funded ('budget') study places, but whether an EU citizen from Denmark can compete for them is not confirmed here; ask the university.
Latvian state-guaranteed student loans are mentioned by SSE Riga as available; eligibility for a Danish citizen is not confirmed here; ask SSE Riga.
Danish SU for a full degree abroad requires approval of the programme by Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen. Check this with your studievejleder.

As an EU citizen bring your EU health insurance card (the blue card, or the Danish yellow card for EU-funded treatment) for necessary care. Latvia's public system covers emergencies; most international students also take out private insurance. Non-EU students must arrange insurance as part of the residence permit application.

As a Danish or other EU/EEA citizen you can travel to Latvia freely and stay three months with no immigration procedure at all. For a longer stay you complete registration formalities with the Office of Citizenship and Migration Affairs and receive a Registration Card. Non-EU students must obtain a residence permit before arriving in Latvia, arranged through the university's international office. After finishing a bachelor's degree, non-EU graduates get four months to find further study or work.

Latvia is a three-hour flight from Denmark, uses the euro, and charges a fraction of what the UK or the Netherlands charge. There is no central admissions system for international students: you apply directly to each university, and the one step you cannot skip is getting your IB Diploma recognised by the Academic Information Centre. The real draw is Riga Stradins University, whose English-taught medicine and dentistry programmes take large numbers of Scandinavian students who did not get a place at home.
Cheap, close to home, and the Nordic route into medicine
English-taught medicine and dentistry at RSU, with no Danish quota standing in the way

Precedent: "The deadline for Non-EU applicants submitting an application towards courses commencing in October 2026, and requiring a visa to travel to Malta, is 1 July 2026 at 14:00." Applications received after it are deferred to the next intake rather than refused. As a Danish or other EU citizen you are not bound by this earlier date and the July main deadline is yours.
Danish SU for a full degree abroad requires programme approval by Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen - check with your studievejleder.

The Maltese Matriculation Certificate that IB is compared against consists of six subjects: two at Advanced Level, three at Intermediate Level, plus Systems of Knowledge. The general entry requirement also includes SEC passes (grade 5 or Level 3) in English, Maltese and Mathematics. UM says these 'may also be satisfied through the subjects presented in the IB Diploma if such subjects are deemed comparable', and a non-Maltese applicant educated abroad 'may be allowed to offer another language instead of Maltese, as approved by the Admissions Board'.

A non-Maltese applicant educated abroad may offer another language instead of SEC Maltese, with Admissions Board approval. Medicine is the exception: non-Maltese M.D. applicants must pass UM's Medical Maltese Proficiency examination.

As a Danish or other EU citizen you have the right to live and study in Malta. If you stay more than three months you register with Identita's Expatriates Unit (on a Study basis) for a residence document, showing your acceptance letter and that you have sufficient means; University of Malta, MCAST and ITS students do not need to show health insurance. It takes about 30 working days. The e-residence permit also gives you free public transport. Non-EU students need a student visa and must apply much earlier - the 2026 visa-applicant deadline was 1 July.
The general entry requirement includes a SEC pass in Maltese. If you were educated abroad you may offer another language instead, but the Admissions Board has to approve it

Danish SU: as a Danish citizen you can normally take SU with you for a full degree abroad. Apply to Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen well before you leave - this is the single most valuable piece of funding for a Danish student in the Netherlands.

Bring your blue European Health Insurance Card from Denmark. If you only study, the EHIC plus your Danish coverage is normally enough. The moment you take a paid job or a paid internship in the Netherlands, Dutch law requires you to take out Dutch basic health insurance (basisverzekering) - Nuffic budgets about 133 EUR a month for it. If you are on Dutch basic insurance and on a low income you can usually claim zorgtoeslag (healthcare allowance) from the tax office, which refunds part of the premium. Register with a local GP (huisarts) early; in student cities the good practices fill up.

The Netherlands is a common choice for Danish IB students: hundreds of bachelor's degrees taught entirely in English, three-year programmes, a statutory tuition fee of 2,694 euro for EU students in 2026/27, and a teaching style built on seminars, group work and reading you are expected to do without being chased. Two things have changed. Parliament is working on a law that pushes bachelor's teaching back towards Dutch, and universities have already started cutting or capping English tracks. And the room shortage is genuinely severe - the national student housing monitor published in 2025 estimated a shortage of about 21,500 student rooms in the 19 largest student cities.

Published as "1 December, the year before you plan to start" — but only for applicants "from outside the Nordic countries" who "cannot document proficiency in Norwegian". A Danish IB student with Danish A at grade 3 or better documents Norwegian and applies through Samordna opptak by 15 April instead, where NMBU requires Norwegian B2 even though the programme is taught in English. Without Danish A, this 1 December route is the one.

The figure of NOK 15,488 per month is formally the immigration authority's subsistence requirement for non-EEA students, but it is also the realistic cost of living and the right number for a Danish student to budget against.

Danish SU at the udeboende rate — DKK 7,426 per month before tax in 2026. Nordic study is paid as if you studied in Denmark, so it draws on the same SU-klip as a Danish degree; under the SU reform that takes effect on 1 January 2027, anyone starting after 1 July 2025 gets SU for the programme's prescribed length only.

Bring your Danish EHIC. It covers medically necessary care from public providers on the same terms as a tourist. Once you are registered as resident with a national identity number you get care on the same basis as Norwegians, including a fastlege (assigned GP). Helsenorge recommends private insurance on top, particularly for repatriation. Taking a job generally makes you a member of folketrygden — check with NAV.
That Maths AA SL alone satisfies R1+R2 is the single most favourable rule in Norway for IB students. In the Danish system the equivalent normally means Matematik A.

The Norwegian language requirement does not apply to programmes taught in English (opptaksforskrifta § 3-8). Institutions do not apply this uniformly, though: NMBU requires Norwegian B2 for its English-taught bachelor's when you apply through Samordna opptak — which Danish A at grade 3 documents.

Settled: Samordna opptak's IB page lists Danish A, higher or standard level, at grade 3 or better as meeting the Norwegian requirement for general admission, alongside Norwegian A and Swedish A. A Danish IB student with Danish A does not need Norskprøven or Bergenstesten.
Also unconfirmed: whether an IB Diploma earned abroad counts as a førstegangsvitnemål for the reserved quota. This materially affects how competitive you are.

Home to the only veterinary education in Norway, and one of very few English-taught entry points for an IB student drawn to ESS, biology and global development. With Danish A you apply through Samordna opptak by 15 April; without it, directly by 1 December 2026.

Norway's oldest and most prestigious university — but for an IB student without Norwegian there is exactly one English bachelor's door, and it wants every document by 1 December 2026. With Danish A, its Norwegian-taught bachelor's are open through Samordna opptak.

Norway's engineering powerhouse and its largest university, with a Nobel-winning neuroscience institute. Every bachelor's is in Norwegian, but Danish A at grade 3 or better documents that for Samordna opptak — so it is open to a Danish IB student willing to study in Norwegian.

Danish and Norwegian are mutually intelligible in writing, so reaching B2 Norwegian is a far smaller undertaking for a Danish student than for most applicants. This is worth taking seriously — it unlocks the whole free system.

Norway charges EU/EEA students no tuition, and your IB converts generously onto the Norwegian scale. The catch is language: NTNU, UiT and several other big universities teach every bachelor's degree in Norwegian, and only about fifteen bachelor's programmes nationally are in English. But Samordna opptak counts Danish A at grade 3 or better as documented Norwegian, so a Danish IB student who takes Danish A can apply to the whole free Norwegian-taught system through one application with ten ranked choices, closing 15 April.
Free, close to home — and almost entirely in Norwegian
English-taught programmes apply direct to the institution and often close on 1 December 2026 — months before Danish or British norms, and before predicted grades are settled.

UiO's one English-taught bachelor's wants every document by 1 December 2026, which a May 2027 candidate cannot meet. NMBU's is open to you through Samordna opptak by 15 April if you document Norwegian, and Danish A does.
Lånekassen is realistically closed to a school-leaver arriving from Denmark, and Norway offers no scholarships to EU/EEA bachelor students.
Danish A at grade 3 or better, HL or SL, meets Samordna opptak's Norwegian requirement, so no Norwegian test is needed for Norwegian-taught programmes.
Danish SU is paid here as if you studied in Denmark, not capped at the four years that apply outside the Nordics.

Teaching starts in late February 2028, which for a May 2027 IB candidate means eight months between the last exam and the first lecture. This is the main New Zealand intake and the one most Danish students will take. The universities publish recurring annual closing dates rather than a national one, and Otago gives 15 November for an offshore international applicant and Victoria University of Wellington 8 December — both are their own entries below. The University of Auckland's general Semester One 2028 date is not published: its 2028 table currently lists only the four clinical health programmes, and its Semester One 2027 equivalent was 8 December 2026, recorded here as precedent and not as a prediction. None of the eight universities had published exact 2028 teaching dates on 23 September 2026.

Otago splits its international applicants in two and gives them different days, and the split is the trap for a Danish student. An offshore applicant — one applying from Denmark — closes on 15 November; an onshore one, already in New Zealand, has until 10 December. Take the later date and you have missed by twenty-five days. Otago published these as 15 November 2026 and 10 December 2026 for semester 1, 2027; the 2028 equivalents are not published, but Otago states that "The main international student application period is 1 May–15 November, for most studies commencing in semester 1 (February)", so 15 November 2027 is expected. Some programmes run different periods — teaching, oral health and dental technology are named — so check yours rather than assuming this date.
Not applicable - New Zealand has no EU/EEA fee category. Danish students pay international fees.
The New Zealand Excellence Awards and similar government-backed schemes target specific countries and regions; check whether Danish students are eligible.
Danish SU may in some circumstances follow you abroad for a full degree. Check su.dk and speak to your studievejleder early.

International students on a student visa are generally not entitled to publicly funded healthcare in New Zealand, so Immigration New Zealand requires acceptable medical and travel insurance for the whole period of study, and universities normally arrange or sell a compliant policy. The EHIC and the Danish yellow card are not valid. Budget for insurance as a separate annual cost.

First-year students are strongly encouraged into university halls of residence, and most universities guarantee a place if you apply by their deadline - take it, because private renting from Denmark is difficult and the halls are where you meet people. Otago is famous for its all-in residential first year in Dunedin. Auckland and Wellington private rents are high; Dunedin, Hamilton, Palmerston North and Christchurch are much more affordable.

A route to a New Zealand bachelor's if your IB total is below the university thresholds. It asks for an IB score of 24 or above for degree entry (the Danish Studentereksamen only for diploma entry); check the degree is at level 7 so the Post Study Work Visa applies, and note that Unitec and Manukau Institute of Technology became one polytechnic on 1 January 2026, so older guidance describes a different entity.

Be clear about what you cannot get. Article 324(3) restricts the Polish maintenance grant (stypendium socjalne) and the Polish student loan (kredyt studencki) to EU citizens who are workers, self-employed, retain a right of residence on that basis, or hold permanent residence. A Danish student who simply arrives to study cannot claim either.

NAWA runs three incoming-student programmes - the gen. Anders Programme, Poland My First Choice, and the Banach Scholarship Programme - but their eligibility rules are not confirmed here. The gen. Anders programme is by name and design aimed at people of Polish descent and Banach at developing countries, so do not assume a Danish student qualifies for any of them without reading the call document.
Danish SU and Danish tuition support are decided in Denmark at su.dk and ufm.dk. Apply early.

As an EU citizen you use your Danish European Health Insurance Card. The national portal states that a valid passport, student identity card and a valid EHIC entitle the holder to medical care free of charge in Poland. Polish residence law also expressly accepts entitlement under EU coordination rules as satisfying the health insurance condition for a student's right of residence. Two cautions: an EHIC is designed for medically necessary treatment during a temporary stay rather than as long-term cover for a resident student, and Polish universities commonly expect either voluntary National Health Fund (NFZ) insurance or private cover. Non-EU students sign a voluntary NFZ agreement costing about 15 EUR a month. The NFZ premium and enrolment route for an EU student are not confirmed here; ask your university. Source: https://study.gov.pl/health-insurance

The Jagiellonian School of Medicine in English publishes a Denmark-specific rule: a Danish school English grade of 7 satisfies its English requirement, alongside Norway 4, Sweden C, Finland 5 and Iceland 8.
Eligibility, amounts and deadlines for the three NAWA scholarship programmes could not be read, so whether a Danish student with no Polish ancestry qualifies for any of them is unknown.

For the first three months you need do nothing beyond holding a valid travel or identity document, under article 15 of the 2006 act on entry and residence of EU citizens. Beyond three months you have a right of residence as a student under article 16(3) provided you have sufficient funds not to become a burden on social assistance and you have health insurance - and the article expressly accepts entitlement under EU social security coordination, which is the EHIC route, so your Danish blue card satisfies it. Article 20(1) then obliges you to register your residence, which you do at the voivodeship office for where you live. The national portal says EU students should apply for registration within 90 days of arrival and are issued a cost-free certificate of registration. The detailed procedure, forms and processing time are not confirmed here; ask the voivodeship office. Sources: https://study.gov.pl/visa-application and https://lexlege.pb.pl/ustawa-o-wjezdzie-na-terytorium-rzeczypospolitej-polskiej-pobycie-oraz-wyjezdzie-z-tego-terytorium-obywateli-panstw-czlonkowskich-unii-europejskiej-i-czlonkow-ich-rodzin/art-20/

If you study medicine here and then want to work in Denmark, the diploma alone is not enough. Poland's entry in Annex V of the EU professional qualifications directive requires the LEK state exam certificate, and the Polish medical chamber says it can only certify full qualifications if you also have a recognised postgraduate internship. See the medicine-abroad page before you commit.
Poland's maintenance grant and student loan are closed to a Danish student who is not working in Poland, under article 324(3) of the Higher Education Act. Your funding has to come from Denmark.
The Jagiellonian School of Medicine in English has an explicit Denmark rule: a Danish English grade of 7 satisfies its English requirement.
Listed for completeness. A Danish citizen is NOT eligible for this route. U.Porto offered 712 places across this contest for 2026/27.
A Danish citizen is NOT eligible for this route.

Published as "From November 10 to December 4, 2026, until 5.00 pm Lisbon time"; the time is the closing time. Same eligibility rule: international student status does not apply to EU or EEA nationals, so a Danish citizen cannot use this route. It is listed because it falls in this window and is easy to mistake for an EU-open one.

Published as "From April 14 to June 16, 2026, until 5.00 pm Lisbon time"; the time is the closing time. A Danish citizen may NOT use this route. The page states that international student status does not apply to nationals of an EU Member State or of a state signatory to the EEA Agreement, so an EU applicant to Nova SBE goes through the Concurso Nacional de Acesso instead. Listed for completeness. The spring intake is a separate entry.

This is the deadline that applies to an IB candidate, and it is a week earlier than the one everybody else sees. DGES's Portuguese calendar page names the group as "candidatos com pedido de substituição de provas de ingresso por exames estrangeiros" and gives them 20 a 29 de julho, against 20 de julho a 06 de agosto for the rest. If you are asking a Portuguese university to accept IB subjects in place of the Portuguese provas de ingresso — which is the normal route for a Danish IB candidate — you are in this group. The 2026 calendar was approved by Despacho n.º 9359-A/2026 of 23 July 2026; the 2027 calendar will be approved by its own despacho and is not published yet.
Nationals of Portuguese-speaking (CPLP) countries can get reductions of up to 45% on international-statute fees — not relevant to a Danish student, but it explains fee tables you will see.
Danish SU may be taken abroad for a full degree if the programme is approved — check su.dk first.

Travel on your Danish passport or ID card. For stays over three months, EU citizens register at the local câmara municipal and receive a Certificado de Registo de Cidadão da União Europeia. You will also need a NIF (tax number) from the Finanças office almost immediately — rental contracts, bank accounts and phone contracts all require it.

Portugal has two completely separate front doors, and a Danish student must use the national one. Non-EU students use the Estatuto do Estudante Internacional, apply straight to a university, and pay somewhere between €3,500 and €16,500 a year. EU citizens — including Danes — are legally excluded from that route and must go through the Concurso Nacional de Acesso, the same national contest Portuguese school-leavers use. The payoff is the price: the capped public tuition (propina) was €697 for 2025/26. The catch is that the national contest is built around Portuguese school exams and mostly leads to Portuguese-taught degrees.

One day, three things. As a Danish citizen you pay no application fee and no tuition, but you do not get the exemption automatically — you have to document your EU/EEA citizenship by this date, and University Admissions handles that on the same deadline it uses to collect the fee from everyone else. All supporting materials are due the same day.

Danish SU: because Sweden is a Nordic country, SU and SU loans for a full degree are paid as if you studied in Denmark, not capped at the four years that apply outside the Nordics. Under the SU reform that takes effect on 1 January 2027, anyone starting after 1 July 2025 gets SU for the programme's prescribed length only. You must be a Danish citizen, or an EU/EEA citizen with sufficient ties to Denmark.

As a Danish EU citizen, carry your EU health insurance card for necessary care. Once you register with Skatteverket and get a personnummer you use the normal Swedish system with the usual patient fees. Non-EU students must hold comprehensive health insurance for studies under one year; for longer permits they are normally covered once registered.

The Swedish-language requirement for Swedish-taught programmes can be met with Language and Literature A or Literature A in Swedish, Danish or Norwegian at HL or SL with grade 4 or higher. Danish A counts.
SU

Sweden's other big engineering school, closely tied to Gothenburg's automotive and maritime industries. Its bachelor's degrees are in Swedish and need Swedish 3 - which Danish A at grade 4 or higher meets.
Swedish-taught programmes need Swedish 3 level. Danish Language A or Literature A at HL or SL with grade 4 satisfies it, which is a real advantage for a Danish IB student.
As a Danish speaker you already meet the Swedish-language entry requirement with Danish Language A at grade 4 or higher, which opens Swedish-taught programmes too.

A second decision point, after the offer. NTU set 17 July 2026 as the date by which a 2026 entrant had to say whether they accepted their place with or without the Tuition Grant. The 2027 equivalent is not published yet — but note where in the year it falls: eleven days after IB results, in the middle of the Danish summer.

NTU takes your application on predicted grades and then requires the actual results within three days of release, in the middle of the Danish summer holiday. NUS is gentler and tells IB applicants sitting the May 2027 session that they will hear by the third week of July, and its own three-day rule names Advanced Placement, Gaokao, HKDSE, Indian Standard 12 and STPM and does not name the IB. LASALLE, by contrast, closed the previous November and never sees your results before it decides. The date is the IB's usual results day and is not yet confirmed by the IB for 2027.

NTU does not publish a calendar date. It says actual IB results must be submitted within three days of the results release in July 2027, and the IB releases on 6 July 2027, so 9 July 2027 is arithmetic on those two facts rather than a date NTU has printed. It is a very tight deadline and it lands in the Danish summer holiday. NTU also makes it mandatory to grant it direct access to your official transcripts through the IBO before July 2027, which is a separate action you take months earlier.
Singapore does not differentiate by EU status — the categories are Singapore Citizen, Singapore Permanent Resident and International Student. A Danish student is an International Student.
ASEAN Undergraduate Scholarships and similar regional awards are not open to Danish citizens.

International students are normally required to be covered by the university's own medical insurance scheme, charged as a compulsory fee alongside tuition. Singapore's healthcare is not free at the point of use, and your Danish EHIC does not apply. Check what the university scheme actually covers — it is usually hospitalisation rather than routine care.

EU citizenship gives no advantage. Once you accept an offer, the university sponsors your Student's Pass application through ICA's SOLAR system, which must be completed before you travel. On arrival you complete formalities at ICA and receive the pass. Danish citizens do not need a visa to enter Singapore as a visitor, but you cannot study on a visitor pass.
Denmark’s SU works differently for a full degree outside the EU/EEA. Check su.dk early.

Actual IB results are due at NTU within three days of release — the first week of July, in the middle of the Danish summer holiday. Both NTU and NUS make it mandatory to authorise the IB to release your transcript to them (NUS institute code 000690); ask your IB coordinator before July.
Slovenian citizens, EU citizens including Danes, and Slovenes abroad

Precedent: the 2026/2027 non-EU handbook (rokovnik) was published on 27 January 2026, the first non-EU application period closed on 18 March 2026, and results followed on 27 August 2026 — a month later than the EU results. Applications go through the same eVS portal but the timetable and the contact differ; the University of Ljubljana routes non-EU applicants to admission@uni-lj.si rather than to the central VPIS office. One quirk runs the other way: the University of Ljubljana leaflet states that the English-taught Business and Economics degree at the Faculty of Economics may be chosen only in the non-EU rounds and by Slovenes abroad, so an EU applicant cannot select it in the ordinary EU round at all.

Precedent: 24 July 2026 for Slovenian and EU citizens whose evidence was complete by 10 July, 5 August 2026 for Slovenes abroad, 27 August 2026 for non-EU citizens, and 18 September 2026 for anyone admitted late in the first round. The decision is not posted to you: you read it by logging in to your own application at portal.evs.gov.si. Your enrolment window opens when it appears, and it is short.

The leaflet, in Slovene: "Kandidati, ki so sprejeti v prvem roku, se vpisejo od 24. julija do najkasneje 14. avgusta 2026; naknadno sprejeti do 30. septembra 2026; sprejeti v drugem prijavnem roku in v roku za zapolnitev mest do 30. septembra 2026." The first-round window is about three weeks across late July and early August, it runs straight through the Danish summer holidays, and enrolment happens at the faculty rather than centrally — "Vpis poteka na fakultetah in akademijah", which contact you in writing or by e-mail. Plan to be reachable, and to be able to get to Ljubljana in the first half of August if your faculty asks you to come in person.
A Public Call for Scholarships for Foreign Citizens exists but is aimed at Western Balkan postgraduate students, so it is unlikely to help a Danish IB applicant.
Danish SU for a full degree abroad requires programme approval by Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen; check with your studievejleder.

As a Danish EU citizen you are covered for necessary care with an EHIC. Students without EU/EEA or bilateral-agreement cover must buy compulsory Slovenian health insurance at EUR 126.33 a month (8.2% of average gross earnings), and the national portal recommends supplementary private insurance on top because the compulsory cover is only partial.

The national Study in Slovenia portal states the obligation flatly and names no exemption at all: a candidate who finished school abroad "is obliged to acquire a decision on the recognition of the foreign education, if they have not obtained one already". It does not mention the International Baccalaureate anywhere.
One: Business and Economics at the School of Economics and Business - but the 2026/2027 call let it be chosen only in the non-EU rounds and by Slovenes abroad, not in the EU round.

Very limited. About 17 English-taught bachelor programmes across the four public universities: University of Primorska 10 (Tourism; Tourism destination management; Anthropology; Cultural Heritage; Academic Bachelor in Management; Bioinformatics; Computer Science; Mathematics; Mathematics and Computer Science; Wood Innovation for Sustainability); University of Maribor 5 (Contemporary Tourism Practices; Economic and business sciences; Business administration; Economic and Technical Logistics; System logistics); University of Nova Gorica 1 (Physics and Astrophysics); University of Ljubljana 1 (Business and Economics, which the 2026/2027 call opened only to non-EU citizens and Slovenes abroad). Colleges and private institutions add about fifteen more, among them Alma Mater Europaea (eight), the College of Management Bled, the Academy of Visual Arts, NOA and GEA College.
Applying is not enrolling. Slovenia decides the first round on 24 July and expects you to enrol at the faculty by mid-August, and both of those dates land inside the Danish summer holidays.

Slovenia has an unusual system called studentsko delo - student work through official Student Services, using a referral document ('napotnica'). Minimum referenced pay is EUR 7.21 an hour, with a 15.5% pension and disability deduction for all students, leaving about EUR 6.20. Foreign students additionally have 22.5% withheld as income tax prepayment, reclaimable if your home country has a double taxation treaty with Slovenia. Weekly or monthly hour limits, and any EU/non-EU eligibility difference, were not stated on the page read on 2026-09-22.

Published as "Final, official transcripts must be postmarked or electronically submitted". This is a condition of an offer you have already accepted, so missing it costs the place rather than the application. Your gymnasium sends it, not you, and a Danish school in the first week of July is a quieter place than it is in June — ask for it before the summer.

What you need to know about Early Decision is not when it closes but what signing it costs you. Early Decision I (1 to 15 November 2026) and Early Decision II (early January 2027) are binding in the strongest sense the American system has. Amherst's wording is that you agree not to be an Early Decision candidate anywhere else and, if admitted, to withdraw your applications from every other college and enrol. It is a signed agreement — student, parent and school counsellor — filed inside the Common App for one college only. Two consequences follow and neither is obvious from a calendar. First, an admitted Early Decision applicant does not get the 1 May reply date: that decision was made in November. Second, and for a Danish family paying from abroad this is usually the more expensive loss, you can never compare financial aid offers, because you will only ever hold one. Early Action, Restrictive Early Action and Single-Choice Early Action are NOT binding — you keep every offer and still reply on 1 May — but Stanford's and Yale's restrict where else you may apply early, so they still decide your whole autumn in October. Missing an early round costs you that round's higher admit rate; signing an Early Decision agreement costs you the choice.

Each institution's aid deadline is its own, and at most of them it is the application deadline itself. Grinnell states that "All financial aid forms must be submitted by the same deadline as the Common Application". Macalester states that "financial aid cannot be awarded after an offer of admission has been made, nor at any time during their studies at Macalester" — that is a door that closes permanently, not a late penalty. Bowdoin's Regular Decision aid deadline is 1 February, a month after its application date. MIT's two aid dates, 30 November and 15 February, have entries of their own. A family that applies first and asks about money in the spring has forfeited the money. Which form: as a Danish citizen you file the CSS Profile, not the FAFSA. The FAFSA is the United States federal aid application and federal aid requires US citizenship or eligible-non-citizen status, which an F-1 student visa is not — so every FAFSA date you will meet on American admissions pages, including the 1 October opening and the 2 March deadline printed on the University of California's own dates page, is not yours. Grinnell asks for "the 2027-28 CSS Profile"; Macalester asks for the CSS Profile "OR the 2027-2028 International Student Application for Financial Assistance (ISAFA)" and points international applicants who cannot afford the CSS Profile fee at the free ISAFA instead, because neither college waives the CSS Profile fee for international applicants. The CSS Profile itself carries no national deadline — the colleges set them, typically 1 or 15 November for the early rounds and January to February for Regular Decision. The College Board had not published the 2027-28 opening date on 23 September 2026; the customary opening is 1 October of the preceding year. Open the CSS Profile in early October 2026 and check the date yourself.
Not applicable - the United States does not have an EU/EEA fee category. As a Dane you pay the international or out-of-state rate everywhere.

Athletic scholarships (NCAA). Real but narrow. Division I and II programmes can offer athletic money; Division III, which includes most liberal arts colleges, cannot offer any athletic aid at all. You must register with the NCAA Eligibility Center and be recruited by a coach - you cannot apply for an athletic scholarship the way you apply for a grant. For a Danish IB student this is realistic only in sports where you already compete at national level, typically rowing, swimming, football, handball, golf or tennis.

Danish SU. Danish state education support can in some circumstances follow you abroad for a full degree. Rules are set by Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen - talk to your studievejleder and check su.dk early, because the application has its own deadlines.

Health insurance is compulsory and expensive, and the Danish yellow card and EHIC are worthless in the US. Universities charge their own student health plan unless you can prove equivalent cover - Harvard's is 4,954 USD and Berkeley's SHIP 5,066 USD for 2026-27. Private Danish travel or study insurance sometimes qualifies for a waiver, but the university decides and the waiver deadline is usually 1 July. Assume you will pay for the university plan.

An American bachelor's degree takes four years and starts broad: you take courses across several fields and usually declare a major at the end of year two. Admission is 'holistic' - your grades matter most, but so do essays, teacher references, what you do outside school, and increasingly again the SAT or ACT. As a Danish student you are an international applicant everywhere, so you pay the published sticker price unless a university gives you financial aid, and only a handful of universities give internationals enough aid to make it affordable. The cost range is enormous: for 2026-27 a full year runs from about 62,000 USD for an international student at Illinois to 95,000-100,000 USD at Harvard before health insurance.
